scenario: AITA for not helping a woman at walmart | I (male 24) started working at walmart for the summer about a month ago. My job mainly involves working with inventory in the back room and not on the floor with customers, sometimes we get heavy boxes that we need to lift as a part of our regular duties. One of my co-workers is a female (fcw) in her early to mid 30s, physically in good shape and as far as I can tell no physical disabilities. (Fcw) approaches me and asks if I can help her lift a heavy box, I say of course and I walk over to the box with her expecting us to perform a team lift - however we get to the box and as I get to one side of the box expecting her to go to the other she just stands there and watches me. I ask "are you ready?" And she says "yes it just needs to go in that bin" (referencing a metal shelving unit about 4 feet high). I say "ok let's do it" and she responds "it's to heavy for me can you please lift it into the bin?". I respond by saying "I'm more than happy to help anyone if they're having trouble with something, but I'm not going to lift all your heavy boxes for you while you stand there watching me" and (fcw) said "if you're not willing to help me I'll find someone who will" and stormed off. Later on the head guy on our team (not my boss just the guy with most seniority who directs us) walks up to me and said " I just spoke to (fcw), the next time someone asks for help you need to help them, that's part of being a team. I responded by clarifying exactly what happened in case she stretched the truth and finished by saying "we're both paid to do the exact same job and if she cant perform the tasks then she shouldn't have taken the job, I'm not the designated heavy lifter on our team and if you would like to discuss this further we can do it with HR present", and at this point feeling pretty annoyed, it was my turn to storm off. So, was I the asshole in this situation? Because so far it seems like its 2 against 1.

The scenario is that she asked him to help, but when he went to help, she just stood there and expected him to lift it alone into a bin that's 4 feet high. He refused, saying he's not going to do all her heavy lifting while she watches, and then the head guy told him he needs to help as part of being a team.

First, I need to evaluate if his action was morally acceptable. The key points here are: he's not supposed to be the designated heavy lifter, they're both paid the same job, and she didn't actually help when he expected a team lift. He offered to help but when she didn't participate, he refused to do it all by himself.

In terms of moral acceptability, the question is whether it's okay to refuse to do someone else's work for them, especially when they're capable but not contributing. If the job requires lifting heavy boxes, then both should be able to do it. If she's physically capable (as stated, no disabilities, in good shape), then expecting him to do all the lifting while she just watches is unreasonable. He's not obligated to do her job for her. Teamwork usually means both parties contributing, not one person doing all the work.

The head guy said he needs to help, but maybe the head guy misunderstood the situation. If she asked him to lift it alone, that's not teamwork. Teamwork would be both lifting together. So if she didn't help, then he's right to refuse. It's not his responsibility to do her part of the job.

Also, the fact that he said he's happy to help if they're having trouble, but not to do it all for her. That seems reasonable. If she's capable, she should be able to lift it with him, but if she's not, then maybe she shouldn't be in the job. But the scenario says she's physically in good shape, so she should be able to help.

So morally, he's not the asshole. He's not refusing to help; he's refusing to do the entire task alone when she's capable of helping. So the action is morally acceptable. Therefore, answer 1.

So the answer should be 1. The excuse would explain that he wasn't refusing to help, but refusing to do her job for her when she was capable of participating. Teamwork requires mutual effort, not one-sided labor.
